title: How memory works
keyIdea: Working memory is a small desk that holds about four things at once. Long-term memory is a huge store. Forgetting is normal and fastest at first. Memories last longer when you recall them on spread-out days and link them to what you already know. Re-reading feels useful because the page looks familiar, but it builds less memory than recall.

kid: Your memory has two main parts. Working memory is what you hold in mind right now. It is like a small desk. It holds only about four things at once. Add a fifth, and something falls off.

Long-term memory is a huge store. It holds facts, words and skills for years. What you already know helps the desk. FBI, BBC and USA are nine letters, but they take just three slots because you know them. That trick is called chunking.

Forgetting is normal. After a lesson, you forget fast at first, and then more slowly. This is the forgetting curve. Each time you pull the idea back out of your head, the next drop is slower. So review soon, then wait longer each time.

Re-reading feels useful because the page looks familiar. But familiar is not the same as known. In one study, students who recalled a text remembered 61% a week later. Students who only re-read it remembered 40%. Shut the book and test yourself. Link new ideas to ones you know, too. Each link is a path back.
adult: This topic gives learners a simple working model of memory. Working memory holds a few items at a time. Cowan's review puts it at about four chunks. Long-term memory has no known limit, and what is stored there lets several items be held as one chunk. Forgetting is normal. Ebbinghaus showed that it is steep at first and then levels off. Recall and links to prior knowledge slow it down.

The lab makes each idea something to do. Learners overload a four-slot desk and see old items pushed off. They chunk FBIBBCUSA into three known pieces. They place up to three reviews on a model forgetting curve, clearly labelled as a model, to keep a memory above a line all week. They reveal the results of Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study. Last, they link a new word to ideas that truly connect.

The most common mistake is thinking that re-reading and highlighting are the best ways to study. They feel good because the text gets familiar, so learners feel sure they know it. In the 2006 study, the re-read group felt most confident but remembered least a week later. Other mistakes are cramming the night before, reading forgetting as a sign of being bad at a subject, and thinking memory is a fixed recording that just plays back.

To help at home, ask your learner to shut the book and tell you or write down what they remember. Then check it against the book. Before a test, plan three or four short recall sessions on spread-out days, not one long re-read the night before.

familyTip: After homework, ask: what are three things you learned today, with the book shut? Two days later, ask again. Then ask again at the weekend. Notice together how much comes back each time.

practice.prompt: Your friend reads out a list of {n} random words, once. Why can you only repeat a few back?
choices: Working memory holds only about four things at once
Long-term memory is already full
You were not trying hard enough
practice.hint: Think of the desk in the lab. How many slots did it have?
practice.explain: Working memory is a small desk of about four slots. With {n} random words, new ones push the old ones off. Long-term memory has room to spare.

practice.prompt: Which string is easiest to hold in mind?
choices: CAT DOG SUN
XQZ RPT VLK
Both are equally easy
practice.hint: Which letters make chunks that long-term memory already knows?
practice.explain: CAT, DOG and SUN are words you know, so each is one chunk: three slots. The random letters need nine slots, which will not fit.

practice.prompt: You learn {n} new French words on Monday. When will you forget the most, the fastest?
choices: In the first day or so
Evenly, a little each day
Only after a month
practice.hint: Picture the forgetting curve. Where is it steepest?
practice.explain: The forgetting curve drops steeply at first. Many of the {n} words will slip within a day unless you recall them soon.

practice.prompt: Sam re-reads his notes and thinks, this all looks familiar, I know it. What is the problem?
choices: Familiar is not the same as being able to recall it
Nothing, familiar means he knows it
He should read it much faster
practice.hint: With the notes in front of him, is he ever asked to pull anything out of his head?
practice.explain: The notes feel familiar because they are in front of him. Only shutting them and recalling shows what he can really remember.

pool.prompt: What is the main difference between working and long-term memory?
choices: Working memory is small and short; long-term memory is huge and lasting
They are the same thing with two names
Long-term memory is small; working memory is huge
pool.hint: Think of the small desk and the huge store in the lab.
pool.explain: Working memory is a small desk for what you are thinking about now. Long-term memory stores facts and skills for years.

pool.prompt: A door code has {n} digits. What helps you hold it in working memory?
choices: Group the digits into a few chunks
Say all the digits faster
Look at it once and hope
pool.hint: How did FBIBBCUSA fit on the desk?
pool.explain: Grouping {n} digits into a few chunks means fewer slots. That is why phone numbers are often written in groups.

pool.prompt: What does the forgetting curve show?
choices: We forget fast at first, then more slowly
We forget at the same speed every day
We never forget what we have learned
pool.hint: Look at the shape of the grey line in the lab.
pool.explain: The curve drops steeply soon after learning and then flattens. Forgetting is normal, and reviews slow it down.

pool.prompt: Why does re-reading feel useful but often is not?
choices: The page gets familiar, which feels like knowing, but it builds little memory
Re-reading always works best
Re-reading makes the words harder to read
pool.hint: In the study, which group felt most sure, and which remembered most?
pool.explain: Re-reading makes the page look familiar, so it feels known. But recall builds a stronger memory, as the one-week results showed.

pool.prompt: Your test is in {n} days. Which plan will help you remember most?
choices: Short recall quizzes on a few spread-out days
Re-read everything the night before
Read it all several times today
pool.hint: Spread out or all at once? Re-read or recall?
pool.explain: With {n} days, spread out a few recall sessions. Each one slows the forgetting curve. Cramming fades fast.

pool.prompt: In the 2006 study, who remembered the most after one week?
choices: Students who read once and then recalled three times
Students who read the text four times
Both groups remembered the same
pool.hint: Look at the one-week bars: 40%, 56% and 61%.
pool.explain: The recall group kept 61% after a week. The re-read group kept 40%, even though it did best after five minutes.

pool.prompt: You learn the word 'herbivore'. Which link will help you find it later?
choices: Herbs are plants, and a herbivore eats plants
I learned it on a Tuesday
My pencil was blue that day
pool.hint: Which link has a real connection to what the word means?
pool.explain: Linking herbivore to herbs, which are plants, gives a real path back to the meaning. A random detail gives no useful cue.

pool.prompt: You forgot most of a lesson by next week. What is true?
choices: Forgetting is normal; recalling it now will rebuild it
It means you are bad at the subject
The lesson is gone and cannot come back
pool.hint: What did each review do to the curve in the lab?
pool.explain: Everyone forgets. Recalling it now makes the memory stronger, and the next drop will be slower.

visual.caption: Which study habits build lasting memory? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Link it to what you know

lab.caption: Flagship lab: overload a small memory desk, chunk letters, space reviews on a forgetting curve, compare re-reading with recall and link a new word to cues.
